core: The working definition of a journal entry: the chronological record of a transaction with its debits and credits, attributed to OpenStax's Principles of Accounting and CFI
The parts of an entry, each in one line: date, accounts, debit amounts, credit amounts, description
A simple entry shown in words with an original example (a shop receives cash for a sale: debit Cash, credit Sales Revenue)
Compound entries: one entry with more than two lines when a transaction touches more than two accounts
Why the journal comes first: it is the book of original entry, the general practice
Journal vs ledger: chronological detail vs sorted totals (general-ledger is a sibling topic, referenced only)
The honest framing: an entry is a promise — it must balance (debits equal credits) or it is wrong
supporting: Journalizing is the second step of the accounting cycle, after transactions are identified and analyzed (OpenStax 3.3 and 3.5; CFI Accounting Cycle)
The formatting practice: debit titles first on the left, credit titles after them and indented on the right, at least one debit and one credit, description after each entry (OpenStax 3.5)
Source documents such as sales receipts and invoices are the original evidence behind entries (OpenStax 3.3)
In modern practice, accounting software records entries and updates ledgers together, though the journal-first concept remains (CFI Journal Entry)
outOfScope: The rules of debits and credits per account type (sibling topic: accounting:foundations:debits-and-credits; referenced only)
The general ledger's structure, T-accounts, and posting mechanics (sibling topic: accounting:foundations:general-ledger; referenced only)
The full accounting cycle and its remaining steps (sibling topic: accounting:foundations:accounting-cycle; referenced only)
The trial balance and error correction across accounts (sibling topic: accounting:foundations:trial-balance; referenced only)

claims.claim: A journal is the first place information is entered into the accounting system and is traditionally called the book of original entry, because it is where transaction information originally enters the system.

A journal keeps a historical account of all recordable transactions a company has engaged in, and CFI describes the journal as the company's official accounting record of all transactions documented in chronological order — the basis for the working definition 'the chronological record of a transaction with its debits and credits'.

Every journal entry names the accounts affected with at least one debit and at least one credit, and the dollar value of the debits must equal the dollar value of the credits, or the accounting equation goes out of balance.
A simple entry has exactly one debit account and one credit account; a compound entry has more than one account listed under the debit and/or credit column of a journal entry.

The standard entry format: a date, debit account titles first and on the left, credit account titles after all debit titles and indented on the right, at least one debit, always at least one credit, and a short description written after each entry.
Journalizing (recording journal entries) is the second step in the accounting cycle, following the identification and analysis of transactions from source documents.

The general ledger is a record of each account and its balance; reviewing journal entries individually can be tedious and time-consuming, while the ledger lets a company easily extract account balances — the distinction between the journal's chronological detail and the ledger's sorted totals.

For every journal entry, debits and credits must be equal to maintain balance in the accounting equation; entering an entry involves considering which accounts are affected, whether each increases or decreases, by how much, and whether the equation stays in balance.
Most modern companies use accounting software to enter journal entries rather than keeping manual journals, though understanding the manual form remains part of accounting fundamentals.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Whether the journal is still kept as a physical first record in practice.
positions: CFI notes that while journals were the primary way of recording transactions in the past, most modern companies use accounting software to enter journal entries
OpenStax teaches the journal as the first place information enters the accounting system and the book of original entry
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson teaches the journal-first concept as the general practice and the conceptual book of original entry, and notes that in software the recording and posting steps often happen together.

conflictingEvidence.issue: How the chronological feature of the journal is worded across sources.
positions: CFI explicitly says the journal documents transactions in chronological order
OpenStax describes the journal as keeping a historical account of all recordable transactions without using the word 'chronological' in the extractable text
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson's working definition attributes the chronological wording to the combination of OpenStax (historical account, in-order recording) and CFI (chronological order), so the definition is supported by both.
